Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

derivations.claim: Since $e_0$ is a unit vector, $J_a^{\dagger}J_a=I$ and $J_aJ_a^{\dagger}=\Pi_a$. Therefore $J_a^{\dagger}(\Pi_aU\Pi_a)J_a=J_a^{\dagger}UJ_a=B_U$ and $\Pi_aU\Pi_a=J_aB_UJ_a^{\dagger}$. Thus $J_a$ identifies the restriction of $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ on its range with $B_U$.

The padding conditions give $E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}E_{\rm in}=I_n$ and $E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}=I_m$. Thus $P_{\rm in}:=E_{\rm in}E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}$ is a self-adjoint idempotent. For every $z$, $P_{\rm in}z$ and $(I-P_{\rm in})z$ are orthogonal, so $\|P_{\rm in}z\|^2\le\|z\|^2$. By [F4], $\|E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}z\|^2=\langle P_{\rm in}z,z\rangle=\|P_{\rm in}z\|^2$ and $\|E_{\rm in}x\|^2=\langle x,E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}E_{\rm in}x\rangle=\|x\|^2$. The same adjoint identity gives $\|E_{\rm out}y\|^2=\langle y,E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}y\rangle=\|y\|^2$. Thus the input adjoint is contractive and both padding maps preserve length.

For $a=1$ and $U=X\otimes I_d$, where $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, the displayed matrix satisfies $X^{\dagger}X=XX^{\dagger}=I$, so $U$ is unitary, but $\Pi_aU\Pi_a=0$. Hence the full projected operator need not be unitary.

For a unit $z\in\mathbb C^d$, if $E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}z\ne0$, normalize that vector in the maximum defining [F3]; if it is zero, its image under $A$ is zero. In either case, $\|E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^{\dagger}z\|\le\|A\|_{\rm op}\|E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}z\|\le\|A\|_{\rm op}$, so $\|\widehat A\|_{\rm op}\le\|A\|_{\rm op}$. Conversely, for each unit $x\in\mathbb C^n$, $E_{\rm in}x$ is unit and $\|\widehat A E_{\rm in}x\|=\|E_{\rm out}Ax\|=\|Ax\|$. Taking suprema yields $\|\widehat A\|_{\rm op}=\|A\|_{\rm op}$ by [F3].

derivations.claim: The zero-ancilla coordinate projection $J_a^{\dagger}$ has norm at most one: it discards all coordinates orthogonal to $e_0\otimes\mathbb C^d$, so the squared length of the retained coordinates is at most the squared length of the full vector. It also records whether the family SELECT unitary $\sum_j |j\rangle\langle j|\otimes U_j$ is supplied as one oracle or must be assembled from the separately controlled calls. For every supplied circuit operation $O$, the instance records the applicable circuit-description length, gate count and gate set, depth, total width, and clean and dirty work-ancilla counts; for a uniform family it records the full-description generator time. It separately records each named oracle-query count, classical postprocessing time and space, matrix-data and coefficient-table reading or storage, state-preparation cost, and target precision and its bit encoding when the task is approximate. The cost of a SELECT implementation includes its controls and relative phases unless those are listed as separate supplied primitives. derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F4], the supplied operation $U^{\dagger}$ from [F2] has compression $J_a^{\dagger}U^{\dagger}J_a=(J_a^{\dagger}UJ_a)^{\dagger}=B_U^{\dagger}$. In the rectangular case, $\widehat A^{\dagger}=E_{\rm in}A^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}$, which is exactly the declared padding of $A^{\dagger}$ with the two embeddings exchanged.

For any vector $v$, [F5] and [F6] imply $\|v\|=\max_{\|y\|=1}|\langle v,y\rangle|$: Cauchy–Schwarz gives the upper bound, and if $v\ne0$ the unit vector $y=v/\|v\|$ attains it; for $v=0$ both sides are zero. Therefore, for any endomorphism $T$ of a nonzero finite-dimensional inner-product space, $\|T\|=\max_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle Tx,y\rangle|=\max_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle x,T^{\dagger}y\rangle|=\|T^{\dagger}\|$ by [F3] and exchanging the two unit-vector variables. The zero-dimensional case has both norms zero by [F5].
Apply step 1.2 to $T=B_U-A/\alpha$. Since $\alpha$ is real, [F4] gives $T^{\dagger}=B_U^{\dagger}-A^{\dagger}/\alpha$. Its norm equals $\|T\|\le\varepsilon$, so the block-encoding error is preserved.

derivations.claim: Each lifted operation $V_A,V_B$ is a block-diagonal direct sum of copies of its supplied unitary on the untouched ancilla's computational basis; the inverse is the corresponding direct sum of the component inverse. Thus both lifts and $V_AV_B$ are unitary. Let $J$ inject the system into the all-zero state of both ancillas. The zero-subspace projections are $P_A$ and $P_B$, with $P=P_AP_B$, $PJ=J$, and $J^{\dagger}P=J^{\dagger}$. In $J^{\dagger}V_AV_BJ$, insert $P$ at both ends; commute $P_B$ through $V_A$ and use $P_AV_B=V_BP_A$ to obtain $J^{\dagger}V_AP_BV_BJ$. The vector $P_BV_BJx$ has both ancillas zero and system component $C_Bx$, so $P_BV_BJ=JC_B$. The remaining compression is $J^{\dagger}V_AJC_B=C_AC_B$. Hence the all-zero block is exactly $C_AC_B$ in the stated order.

Set $A':=A/\alpha_A$, $B':=B/\alpha_B$, $E_A:=C_A-A'$, and $E_B:=C_B-B'$. Then $C_AC_B-A'B'=E_AB'+A'E_B+E_AE_B$. By [F1], $\|E_A\|\le\varepsilon_A$ and $\|E_B\|\le\varepsilon_B$; by the normalization promises, $\|A'\|\le1$ and $\|B'\|\le1$. Applying [F3] to each summand yields the first displayed bound, and $\|A\|/\alpha_A,\|B\|/\alpha_B\le1$ yields its conservative final bound.

The same difference can be written $C_AE_B+E_AB'$. By [F4], $\|C_A\|\le1$, so [F3] gives $\|C_AE_B+E_AB'\|\le\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\|B\|/\alpha_B\le\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B$. Also $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|\le\alpha_A\alpha_B$ by [F3]; the product normalization is positive. The block-encoding definition therefore applies with the claimed error.

$$\left\|C_AC_B-\frac{AB}{\alpha_A\alpha_B}\right\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_A\frac{\|B\|_{\rm op}}{\alpha_B}+\varepsilon_B\frac{\|A\|_{\rm op}}{\alpha_A}+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B\le\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B.$$

derivations.claim: Inductively apply [F1] to the first $k-1$ encodings and the $k$th encoding, using disjoint ancillas at every composition. The resulting compression is $B_1\cdots B_k$ in the stated order, and each step multiplies the normalization, giving $\prod_i\alpha_i$.

Put $C_i:=A_i/\alpha_i$, so $B_i=C_i+E_i$. The hypotheses give $\|C_i\|_{\rm op}\le1$. For every unit vector $x$, the vector triangle inequality gives $\|B_ix\|\le\|C_ix\|+\|E_ix\|\le1+\varepsilon_i$; taking the maximum in [F2] yields $\|B_i\|_{\rm op}\le1+\varepsilon_i$.

$$\mathrm{SELECT}:=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes\frac{\beta_j}{|\beta_j|}\,U_j+\sum_{j=m}^{D-1}|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes I,$$

where each $U_j$ acts on its padded component ancilla and the data register; an empty second sum is zero. Return $W:=P^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{SELECT}\,P$, acting on the coefficient register, common component ancillas, and data system.

Write $T^{\dagger}$ for the adjoint $T^*$ characterized by [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]. Fix integers $m,n\ge1$, $a\ge0$, and $d\ge\max(m,n)$. On each coordinate space $\mathbb C^r$ use $\langle x,y\rangle_{\rm root}:=\sum_{q=1}^r x_q\overline{y_q}$, linear in the first argument. Put the ancilla register before the system register in every tensor product, and let $e_0=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ be the first standard basis vector in $\mathbb C^{2^a}$. For $A:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^m$, choose as part of the data padding maps $E_{\rm in}:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^d$ and $E_{\rm out}:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^d$ satisfying $E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}E_{\rm in}=I_n$ and $E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}=I_m$. The default padding sends a coordinate vector to the same coordinates followed by zeros. Set $\widehat A:=E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^{\dagger}:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^d$.

Let $J_a:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^{2^a}\otimes\mathbb C^d$ be $J_ax=e_0\otimes x$, where $e_0$ is the all-zero computational basis vector, and let $\Pi_a:=J_aJ_a^{\dagger}$. The exact case is $\varepsilon=0$. For square $A$, take $m=n=d$ and both embeddings equal to the identity. For rectangular $A$, the dimensions and embeddings remain part of the encoding data.

The equivalent projector notation identifies $B_U$ with the restriction of $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ to $\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_a)$, transported to $\mathbb C^d$ by $J_a$; it does not regard $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ as a unitary.

SELECT is unitary because it is block diagonal on orthogonal index subspaces, with each block a unit-modulus phase times a unitary (and identity on unused labels); hence $W=P^{\dagger}\mathrm{SELECT}P$ is unitary. Projecting SELECT onto the common component-ancilla zero state replaces each $U_j$ by $A_j/\alpha_j$, so the full projected block of $W$ is the coefficient-register matrix element of $P^{\dagger}\bigl(\sum_j|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes(\beta_j/|\beta_j|)A_j/\alpha_j\bigr)P$.

The amplitudes in [F1] are real and nonnegative, so the $(0,j)$ and $(j,0)$ entries of $P^{\dagger}$ and $P$ in this matrix element both equal $\sqrt{w_j}$. Expanding gives $\sum_jw_j(\beta_j/|\beta_j|)A_j/\alpha_j=\sum_j\beta_jA_j/\Lambda$, as claimed.

An **access instance** for a finite family of block-encoding unitaries $U_j$ records, as separate supplied operations, each of $U_j$, $U_j^{\dagger}$, controlled-$U_j$, and controlled-$U_j^{\dagger}$ that an algorithm may call. It also records whether the family SELECT unitary $\sum_j |j\rangle\langle j|\otimes U_j$ is supplied as one oracle or must be assembled from the separately controlled calls. A call to one operation does not imply access to another.

For every supplied circuit operation $O$, the instance records the applicable circuit-description length, gate count and gate set, depth, total width, and clean and dirty work-ancilla counts; for a uniform family it records the full-description generator time. It separately records each named oracle-query count, classical postprocessing time and space, matrix-data and coefficient-table reading or storage, state-preparation cost, and target precision and its bit encoding when the task is approximate. These coordinates follow [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]]; an inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently zero. A bare matrix $A$ supplies none of these circuits or access rights. If an operation is compiled from matrix entries or a coefficient table, its data access, synthesis, precision, and classical costs are recorded separately. The cost of a SELECT implementation includes its controls and relative phases unless those are listed as separate supplied primitives. These block-encoding constructions include no measurement or classical-output step; a consumer's measurement and output costs are accounted separately.

The squared amplitudes sum to one by the definition of $\Lambda$. Define the unitary

$$\mathrm{SELECT}:=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes\frac{\beta_j}{|\beta_j|}\,U_j+\sum_{j=m}^{D-1}|j\rangle\langle j|\otimes I,$$

where each $U_j$ acts on its padded component ancilla and the data register; an empty second sum is zero. Return $W:=P^{\dagger}\,\mathrm{SELECT}\,P$, acting on the coefficient register, common component ancillas, and data system.

Return the unitary $W:=V_AV_B$, so $V_B$ acts first, and use all $a_A+a_B$ ancillas for the projected block. No intermediate measurement or reset is performed. The resulting normalization is $\alpha_A\alpha_B$.

Under the exact inputs and instructions of [[alg-qa-22-lcu-block-encoding]], the all-zero coefficient-index and component-ancilla block of $W=P^{\dagger}\mathrm{SELECT}P$ is

$$\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\beta_jA_j}{\Lambda}.$$

Moreover, $\|\sum_j\beta_jA_j\|_{\rm op}\le\Lambda$, so the constructed unitary is an $(\Lambda,b+a_*,0)$ block encoding of $\sum_j\beta_jA_j$.

Under the inputs and register order of [[alg-qa-22-product-block-encoding]], let $C_A$ and $C_B$ be the two normalized compressed blocks, so $\|C_A-A/\alpha_A\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_A$ and $\|C_B-B/\alpha_B\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_B$. The all-zero block of the constructed unitary is $C_AC_B$. It obeys

$$\left\|C_AC_B-\frac{AB}{\alpha_A\alpha_B}\right\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_A\frac{\|B\|_{\rm op}}{\alpha_B}+\varepsilon_B\frac{\|A\|_{\rm op}}{\alpha_A}+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B\le\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B.$$

Because each $C_A$ is itself a projected unitary block and hence a contraction, the sharper bound $\|C_AC_B-AB/(\alpha_A\alpha_B)\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\|B\|_{\rm op}/\alpha_B\le\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B$ also holds. In particular the product is an $(\alpha_A\alpha_B,a_A+a_B,\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B)$ block encoding of $AB$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

derivations.claim: The errors are $E_A=C_A-A/\alpha_A=\operatorname{diag}(1/10,0)$ and $E_B=C_B-B/\alpha_B=\operatorname{diag}(1/5,0)$. For a diagonal $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2)$, $\|Dx\|^2=|d_1|^2|x_1|^2+|d_2|^2|x_2|^2$, so the maximum on unit vectors is $\max(|d_1|,|d_2|)$, attained at the corresponding basis vector. Hence $\|E_A\|=1/10$, $\|E_B\|=1/5$, $\|A\|_{\rm op}=1/2$, and $\|B\|_{\rm op}=1$. For each of $C_A,C_B$, put $S=\sqrt{I-C^2}$ and $D(C)=\begin{pmatrix}C&S\\S&-C\end{pmatrix}$. The diagonal matrices $C,S$ commute and satisfy $C^2+S^2=I$, so block multiplication gives $D(C)^*=D(C)$ and $D(C)^2=I$. Then [F3] gives $\|D(C)x\|^2=\langle x,D(C)^*D(C)x\rangle=\|x\|^2$, and [F4] makes $D(C)$ unitary; its top-left block is $C$. Thus both chosen compressed blocks have exact unitary dilations.

The theorem's normalized bound is $(1/10)(1/2)+(1/5)(1/2)+(1/10)(1/5)=17/100$. The actual product block is $C_AC_B=\operatorname{diag}(21/50,0)$, whereas $AB/(\alpha_A\alpha_B)=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,0)$; their difference has norm $21/50-1/4=17/100$, so this instance attains that bound.

Multiplying the normalized error by $\alpha_A\alpha_B=2$ gives unnormalized error $17/50$. The looser universal estimate $\varepsilon_A+\varepsilon_B+\varepsilon_A\varepsilon_B=8/25$ also applies but is not tight here.
